changes.name: Fogport Famous
changes.entry:
The Maelstrom is home to millions, but Fogport has always been especially good at making one person’s name everyone else’s business. The following are some of the city’s most recognized personalities, as collected from broadsheets, tram conductors, harbor gossip, licensed histories, tavern arguments, and people who insist they were present.

Not every Fogporter knows every name. A person famous in Blackwake may be unknown in Nine Spoons; a hero of the docks may be cursed in the counting houses. Still, a sharper wick, a careful listener, or anyone who has spent too long in a public house will recognize most of these reputations.

Public Faces

Vauntin Quell, Lord Continuant

Fogport’s ruler is recognized by his silver jaw, his official portraits, and the command stamped beneath his face: BEHOLD. He claims to be a modest servant of the city. The city has been serving him for forty-three years.

Saint Orra of the Last Light

Every sailor, lamplighter, tram conductor, and lost child in Fogport knows the woman beneath the colossal hood. Her raised lamp is supposed to guide the living home. People are less certain what it means when the statue turns its head.

Captain Mirelle Vane, the Burning Pilot

Vane brought thirty-one ships through the Black Gale by setting a road of boats alight across the drowned channels. Dockworkers remember her as a foul-mouthed tugmaster with a broken nose. Government statues keep giving her a spotless naval coat.

Sister Ilyra Fenn of the Red Shawl

Fenn became famous by treating the sick before asking who could pay, then became a legend by opening South Gate during the War of Shut Gates. Her red shawl still hangs above Hushwater Hospital, though the original has been mended so many times that it is mostly thread and intention.

Marden Sile, the Fogwright

Sile designed the enormous intake crowns that draw fog into the Bellworks condensers. He is celebrated as an engineer, blamed as a profiteer, and quietly consulted by anyone whose building has begun breathing through the walls.

Names from the Streets

Mother Salt

Mother Salt sells hot broth beside the harbor and knows which ships arrived before their captains do. She has buried three husbands, adopted nine sailors, and once charged a sea monster for breakfast. The monster paid in pearls and returned every Thursday for six years.

Rook Vellum, the Mapmaker Who Lies Correctly

Vellum sells maps that are wrong in ordinary ways and accurate in dangerous ones. His customers include smugglers, grieving relatives, and Civic Vigilance officers who claim not to know him. He never draws a street he has not personally escaped.

Hester Knell, Undertaker General

Knell’s funeral house has served Fogport since before the Catastrophe, although the building has been replaced twice and one of the replacements was buried with its customers. She is famous for fitting impossible bodies into ordinary coffins and for refusing to hurry the dead.

Orris Pike, the Man with Seven Names

Pike is a respectable importer, a dockside confidence trickster, a former revolutionary, and possibly three different men sharing one hat. He has been arrested under six names and acquitted under the seventh. Nobody agrees which name is his real one, including Pike.

Rattlecap

Rattlecap is a Grig who performs acrobatics on tram roofs while wearing a dinner jacket several sizes too large. Children adore him, conductors detest him, and at least four foreign ambassadors have paid him to deliver messages nobody else could carry through a crowded station.

Old Vesper, Last Lamplighter

Vesper claims to have lit the first gas lamps in Fogport and the last lamp before the Catastrophe. He now carries a ladder through the fog, tending lights that have no visible posts. The Civic Vigilance calls this trespass. The lamps continue to burn.

Infamous Persons

The Gentleman in Rain

No portrait of the Gentleman survives because every artist who finishes one forgets the face before morning. He is blamed for murders, disappearances, and one exceptionally embarrassing diplomatic incident. Whether he is a killer, a title shared by killers, or merely a story used to frighten rich men remains politely unresolved.

Lady Cinder

Lady Cinder runs the most elegant criminal brokerage in Fogport from a succession of buildings that later burn down. She arranges thefts, disappearances, marriages, and occasional reconciliations. Her clients praise her discretion. Her enemies praise it more briefly.

Doctor Pell Soot

Pell Soot is the city’s most notorious unlicensed physician. He has removed bullets, curses, barnacles, memories, and once a small brass bell from inside a magistrate. His patients swear he saved their lives. His former patients are harder to interview.

The Collar Saint

The Collar Saint is a Thrallo who walks the waterfront at night, repairing broken dock chains and leaving food beneath the doors of injured laborers. Some call him a murderer hiding among the poor; others insist he has never harmed anyone. He has never publicly corrected either account.

Madam Widdershins

Widdershins tells fortunes by examining the stains left in teacups, though she has been banned from three tea houses for improving the evidence. Her predictions are usually wrong in detail and alarming in consequence. Civic officials consult her through intermediaries.

The King of Nine Spoons

There is no King of Nine Spoons, and anyone claiming the title is immediately challenged by at least six other claimants. The most persistent is a former eel seller who wears a crown made from bent spoons and has successfully collected taxes from exactly one frightened tourist.

Still Spoken Of

Mercy Vale

Among respectable citizens, Mercy is known as a pawnbroker. In Nine Spoons, she is known as the woman who can find a missing child, a stolen knife, a safe room, or the person who deserves to be afraid. Her reputation is larger than her business and considerably older than her spectacles.

The Gutterkin

They are not one person, but Fogport speaks of them as though they were a single famous household living beneath the city. Every district has a different story: playful thieves, black-eyed angels, cannibals, lost children, or the only creatures brave enough to crawl beneath the Old Palace. Most stories end with the same advice: do not follow them home.

The Thrallo

Every Fogport child knows the dock saying: the crate does not complain, and neither does the Thrallo carrying it. Their strength built much of the modern harbor, yet their names are rarely printed beside the monuments they raised. The city remembers the labor more readily than the laborers.

These are only the famous names. Fogport is crowded with people one astonishing deed, terrible mistake, impossible birth, public scandal, or unusually memorable hat away from joining the list.

More Names Fogport Knows

Brindle Mott, Keeper of the Unclaimed

Mott stores abandoned luggage, drowned cargo, orphaned machinery, and unidentified bones. She can locate almost anything, provided it was once lost by someone important.

Doctor Pellin Varr

Varr treats dockworkers, criminals, Thrallo, Grigs, and anyone who can pay in coin, labor, or secrets. He refuses to amputate until he has tried three stranger solutions.

The Widow Brass

Brass controls Fogport's largest secondhand clothing network. Her garments often contain money, letters, weapons, or evidence belonging to someone still alive.

Hobb Crane, the Man Who Fell Upward

Crane survived a Bellworks accident that threw him through a roof and left him hanging from a zeppelin. He now lectures on industrial safety, usually with screaming demonstrations.

Pallow Green

Green is Fogport's most successful garbage contractor. Aristocrats despise him, rats adore him, and he knows which houses have been empty for less than a day.

Mistress Clatter

Clatter conducts funerals for people whose bodies were never recovered. Several supposedly dead citizens have been forced to attend their own memorials.

The Red Clerk

The Red Clerk approves applications for buildings, marriages, expeditions, and executions that technically do not exist. Nobody remembers the clerk's real name.

Velda Quince, Proprietor of the Last Cup

Quince's teahouse serves sailors, diplomats, smugglers, and exhausted constables. She charges foreigners twice and local liars four times.

Rusk Needle

Needle makes clothing for people too large, too strange, too armed, or too recently dead for ordinary shops. Every unfinished coat waits for its proper wearer.

Barrow Finch, Licensed Scoundrel

Finch's only reliable spell makes nearby locks emotionally attached to their keys. He is respectable because his magic is documented, taxed, and nearly useless.

The Bellwife

The Bellwife claims marriage to the oldest harbor bell. She has no legal status, but harbor workers leave offerings outside her home before storms.

Silas Vire, the Respectable Bastard

Vire teaches ambitious people how to become unforgettable. He is never accused of blackmail because he prefers the word instruction.

Edda Coil

Coil replaced her workforce with machines, then rehired them as machine-tenders, apologizers, and emergency mourners. Investors call her visionary; neighbors call her a curse.

Lady Fennel

Fennel rents a decaying Lastlight mansion to diplomats, escaped criminals, and people hiding from themselves. She insists the house has no ghosts.

Cratch Bellows

Bellows hauls dead fog condensers away from Bellworks. He is famous for dismantling machines everyone else believed were still alive.

Mina Crowglass

Crowglass sings so clearly that people hear her through closed windows and heavy fog. She performs only where someone has recently been abandoned.

Harrow Mace, Champion of the Small

Mace represents tenants, apprentices, beggars, and children against landlords. He has never won a legal argument, but never lost a negotiation.

Tilda Spool

Spool owns the city's respected ropewalk and employs several Gutterkin listed as unregistered apprentices. She is fair, difficult, and dangerous when workers are mistreated.

Father Sallow

Sallow blesses machines rather than people. Drivers bring him broken engines and unlucky pistons. He says machines confess more honestly.

Kettlebell Tom

Tom carried a collapsed warehouse beam for three hours while trapped beneath it. His speeches as a labor negotiator rarely contain more than six words.

Miss Varnish

Varnish restores portraits and changes faces when subjects become politically inconvenient. Clients call her an artist; enemies call her a murderer of history.

The Little Admiral

A Grig child, the Little Admiral commands stolen model boats from a floating market stall. Harbor captains consult him before entering unfamiliar waters.

The Bell-Eyed Woman

She stands beneath the same tram clock every Thursday wearing a veil of brass bells. She knows when every Fogporter will make their next mistake.

The Man Who Owns Tuesday

He sells licenses permitting citizens to use Tuesdays. Nobody has seen the paperwork, but magistrates pay him on Mondays to avoid complications.

Madam Pigeon

Madam Pigeon runs a message service using birds that fly only toward places they have never visited. Her delivery record is excellent.

The Coat Without a Man

A black overcoat walks the Grand Promenade after midnight, bows to grieving widows, and accepts invitations to dinner. It has never been seen empty.

Criminal Names

Creaker Venn, the Door Taxman

Venn collects illegal tolls from doors opening onto profitable rooms, forgotten corridors, or places the city denies exist. He is polite, punctual, and wanted in four districts.

The Candleknife

The Candleknife robs only homes where someone has recently died, claiming the dead have no further use for valuables. He leaves each household one lit candle and never steals from children.

Madam Scrip

Scrip sells forged identities to people who need a new life, then charges extra if the old life is still looking. Her ledger is said to contain the real names of half the waterfront.

Heroes of the City

Captain Odo Vey

Vey commands a tug used to rescue vessels official harbor authorities have abandoned. He has a criminal record in three countries and a medal from four.

Rennick Vale, the Harbor Lantern

Vale has pulled sailors, children, and once an entire mail cart from black water. He says the harbor is not kind; it merely gives him work.

Marra Flint of Serevane

Flint crossed a blockade carrying medicine in a laundry cart and returned for the laundry. She now runs a foreign relief house and refuses gratitude as payment.

Strange Names Still Seen Today

Old Man Soot

Soot appears at every major fire carrying an empty bucket. He is credited with saving hundreds of lives, though nobody has seen him throw water.

Noll the Unwelcome

Noll is a professional guest at weddings, funerals, rallies, and executions. His presence means an event will become historically important.

Vaska Renn of Odrava

Renn sells compact steam engines powerful enough to remove a wall. Mechanics admire them and dislike that they occasionally remember previous owners.

Hrenna Pike of Ulmar

Pike believes the Sayir Sea is changing its mind about Fogport. She is mocked until a prediction proves accurate, after which everyone claims to have supported her.

Ysolde Marr of Keth

Marr is an actress whose performances end before audiences understand what play they attended. Admirers, creditors, and one constable follow her.

Daro Venn of Hask

Venn searches wrecks without crew, maps, or visible equipment. He returns with valuable cargo and boots always wet inside.

Mother Sava of Bellor

Sava travels with a shrine, three assistants, and an enormous collection of keys. Fogport calls her healer, exorcist, smuggler, or thief by the door.

Rian Sol of Veyr

Sol invented a machine that measures civic dishonesty. Three governments confiscated it; the device continues producing results in storage.

Casta Vol of Orsava

Vol rents herself as bodyguard, witness, dance partner, or intimidating dinner guest. Her sword is famous. Her invoices are worse.

Eska Noon of Ravel

Noon delivers letters through sieges, floods, riots, and inverted streets. She never reads a message and remembers every face.

Ula Senn of Merroway

Senn sings only where someone died unexpectedly. Her performances are treated as mourning ceremonies, though she says she is finishing a conversation.

Veyra Lusk of Drom

Lusk purchases condemned buildings seconds before they become valuable. She claims no prophetic gift, only an ear for civic mistakes.

Fogport is full of people one astonishing deed, terrible mistake, impossible birth, public scandal, or unusually memorable hat away from joining this list.
